title: Generalize Place Value Understanding
arc: The census office — restoring the population record, fragment by fragment, until folio one is sealed.
sources: NGSS Science and Engineering Practice 4 (Analyzing and Interpreting Data), grades 3–5 progression: collecting and displaying quantitative data and interpreting it with mathematics — nextgenscience.org, Appendix F
Data Nuggets (MSU KBS LTER, NSF DRK-12 funded): free K–16 activities on authentic large-scale data (populations, survey counts) from real scientific research — datanuggets.org
Playground Architect PBL (Magicore Learning): grade-4 STEM project-based learning explicitly aligned to CCSS 4.NBT.A.1/B.4 — reading and writing large numbers, model making, cost totals

ISTE, 'Classroom AI Projects' (K-12 project guide): students evaluate AI — comparing assistants, using AI to solve problems — mapped to Knowledge Constructor 3.b (evaluate the accuracy, perspective, credibility and relevance of information) and Innovative Designer 4.a (a deliberate design process) — cdn.iste.org AIGDSE_1120

NSTA, 'AI in the Science Classroom' (Sept 2024): the responsible-use rule adopted here — 'Student use of AI should support learning, not replace it… Work generated by AI is not considered the student's own work' — nsta.org/blog/ai-science-classroom

AI4K12 (AAAI + CSTA, NSF DRL-1846073), Five Big Ideas in AI, grades 3–5 band: 'compare answers from two assistants' and ask 'what might the assistant not know? who is missing from the data?' (CA Dept of Ed AI literacy table) — ai4k12.org

Kharashadzi et al., 'Chatbot application in a 5th grade science course' (2021, peer-reviewed): grade-5 students use an AI chatbot as a guide that supplements the teacher — useful, curiosity-raising, a partner for questions, not a replacement — pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8211302

NSTA + STAC, 'Sensemaking in the Age of AI' (2026): AI used 'purposefully and intentionally in service of student learning', in AI-resilient classrooms that 'preserve curiosity, productive struggle, and the habits of thinking'; science and engineering practices as the design frame for AI experiences

prep.title: The census briefing was already at home
prep.lead: Before class, the class met the place-value briefing — the headline numbers and three home questions, at each student's own pace.
prep.goal: Recover the first exposure, so the census work begins with thinking — not with content delivery.
prep.pull: Now the probe: what does the class already hold about place value?

diagnose.title: The gap map for the census office
diagnose.lead: Four checkpoints from the briefing. The class votes what it already holds — we are mapping gaps, not scoring students.
diagnose.goal: Build a gap map: what is known, and what is missing, before the first fragment is restored.
diagnose.pull: Knowledge building closes exactly what the map flags.

practice.title: Practice — feedback in seconds, not days
practice.lead: First with the model open, then with it closed, on the census records. Every answer is met in the moment, not after a delayed correction.
practice.goal: Guided, then independent — learning happens at the moment of doing.
practice.pull: Now a genuinely new situation from the archive. The critic arrives — as a critic, never as an author.

critic.title: A genuinely new situation from the archive
critic.lead: The class defends its place-value method in a situation it has not seen before. AI enters here — as a critic, never as an author.
critic.goal: Transfer the method into new territory and defend it through critique.
critic.pull: One individual task now decides each student's next path.

home: Read this number out loud, seat by seat: 482,106. Say each digit with the seat it sits in.
What is the zero in 482,106 standing for? What would the number be if the zero left its seat?
How many seats lie between the ones and the hundred-thousands? Name each one.

claims: I can read and write numbers up to 10,000 in a place-value chart.
I can say what a digit is worth in the ones, tens, hundreds and thousands.
I can use a zero to hold a place open, like in 305.
I can write a number in expanded form, like 4,215 = 4,000 + 200 + 10 + 5.

independent.prompt: The second damaged record reads 205,306. Which statement is true?
independent.yes: Yes — the 5 sits in the thousands, so it is worth 5,000. The zeros hold the ten-thousands and tens places open.
independent.notYet: Not yet — put 205,306 in the chart and check which seat each digit sits in.

harder.answer: 600,000 + 3,000 + 400 + 8 — the zeros add nothing, but the places they hold open do.
harder.hint: Zeros add nothing — but the places they hold open do.

options.task: An annotated place-value chart: read a surviving census number seat by seat, drawing the chart with every zero labelled as a place held open.
options.stem: ask what each digit is worth → plan the chart's seats → build the drawing → test it by rewriting the number in expanded form → share it at the census desk

options.task: A 45-second read-the-torn-page recording: point at each digit of the restored number and say its place value as you read it. Record it once; the critic will replay it.
options.stem: ask how to read the surviving number → plan the recording → read each digit by its place → test it against the place-value chart → share the clip at the archive desk

options.task: A 60-second presentation backed by a real census fact: ask the AI to name one real district population, verify the figure against a trusted source, and present it with your place-value reading. You verify and you speak — the AI only supplies candidates.
options.stem: ask what a real population looks like → plan the claim → research it with the AI (verify against the trusted source) → build the argument → test it against the place-value rules → share it on the wall

home: Take the number 45. If every digit moved one seat to the left, what would the new number be — and how much would it be worth?
Why is the seat after the ones called the tens? What are the next two seats called?
What happens to a number if every digit moves one seat to the right? Try 360.

claims: I can read and write numbers up to one million in a place-value chart.
I can state both the digit and its value for any place in a number.
I can multiply a whole number by 10 and say where each digit moved.
I can divide a multiple of 10 by 10 and say where each digit moved.

independent.prompt: The key card shows 80,000 = 10 × ?. Which value completes it?
independent.yes: Yes — 8,000 × 10 = 80,000; the 8 moves from the thousands to the ten-thousands.
independent.notYet: Not yet — check both directions: ×10 going left, ÷10 going right.

harder.prompt: A record shows 7,000. Write it as 10 × ?, and again as 100 × ?.
harder.answer: 7,000 = 10 × 700 = 100 × 7 — each seat one place left is worth ten times as much.
harder.hint: Start with 7 and count the seats.

options.task: A movable ten-times staircase: build a physical model where each step left is worth ten times the step below, and slide a single digit up and down it.
options.stem: ask what moving changes → plan the staircase steps → build the model → test it by sliding a digit one seat each way → share it at the census desk

options.task: A ten-times chant the class can clap to: each verse sings one digit's trip one place to the right (ten-times) and one place to the left (one-tenth). Write the words and teach the class the chorus.
options.stem: ask what moving a digit does → plan the verses → write the chant → test it on a classmate (they must rebuild the number) → share it at the census desk

options.task: Redesign the place-value key card with the AI as a number supplier: ask it to propose five new example numbers for each place, check every single one yourself, and lay out the finished card. The AI suggests, you verify, and the card is yours.
options.stem: ask what the key card must show → plan the layout → request example numbers from the AI (verify every one) → build the card → test a classmate with it → share it on the wall

home: Which is greater: 9,999 or 10,000? Which one has more digits — and does that decide it?
Compare 4,371 and 4,381. How many seats do the digits agree on before they disagree?
Make two 5-digit numbers as close together as you can. How close can you get?

claims: I can read and write numbers up to one million in a place-value chart.
I can state the value of each digit in a number.
I can use the symbols for less than and greater than to record which of two numbers is greater.
I can find the first place where two numbers differ.

independent.prompt: The card reads 480,900 or 408,900. Which is the greater number?
independent.yes: Yes — the ten-thousands places differ first: 8 beats 0, so 480,900 is greater.
independent.notYet: Not yet — scan from the greatest place. Which place is the first to differ?

harder.prompt: Which is greater: 999,999 or 1,000,000? Decide it before comparing any digits — and say why that works.
harder.answer: 1,000,000 — it reaches into a place (millions) that 999,999 does not. A number with more digits is always greater.

options.task: A first-difference poster: take two close numbers, display the scan from the greatest place, and mark the single seat that decides which is greater.
options.stem: ask where the comparison will be decided → plan the scan from the left → build the poster → test it with a pair that has embedded zeros → share it on the market wall

options.task: A district map that settles the claim: place both populations on the map, mark where the difference first appears, and draw the evidence so the council can see which clinic location wins.
options.stem: ask which district is really larger → plan the map → compare the digits in order → test the first-difference mark against the numbers → share it at the council table

options.task: A comparison model from a real pair: ask the AI to name two real populations of the same order, verify both figures yourself, build the bar comparison, and label the difference.
options.stem: ask what to compare → plan the model → research a real pair with the AI (verify both figures) → build the bars → test the difference → share it on the wall

home: What is halfway between 3,000 and 4,000? Between 3,200 and 3,300?
The report needs about, not exactly. When do you round up, and when do you round down?
Round 4,861 to the nearest thousand. Which way did it go — and what told you?

claims: I can read and write numbers up to one million in a place-value chart.
I can find the halfway point between two values a place apart.
I can round a number to the nearest ten and to the nearest hundred.
I can decide which side of the halfway point a number sits on.

independent.prompt: The council signs the form for 5,612. It asks for the nearest thousand. Which number goes on it?
independent.yes: Yes — halfway at the thousands is 5,500, and 5,612 sits past it, so it rounds up to 6,000.
independent.notYet: Not yet — find the halfway point of the thousands and see which side 5,612 sits on.

harder.prompt: Round 450 to the nearest hundred. Two students disagree — 400 and 500. Who is right, and what does the class rule say about a number that sits exactly on the halfway point?
harder.answer: 500 — the rule is: at or past halfway, round up. 450 sits exactly on halfway.
harder.hint: The board rule says: at or past it, round up.

options.task: A halfway map: draw the line between two rounded values, mark the halfway point, and place a real number on the right side of it with the rounding written beside it.
options.stem: ask which side of halfway a number sits on → plan the line and the halfway mark → build the map → test it with a number exactly on halfway → share it with the council

options.task: A 60-second 'why this precision is enough' talk: round the district populations to the requested place, defend why that precision is enough for the council's decision, and show the halfway line behind the call.
options.stem: ask how precise the estimate must be → plan the argument → round to the requested place → test it against the halfway line → share it at the council table

options.task: A one-page estimation report on a real number: research one real budget or population figure with the AI, verify it, round it the lesson way, and write the report. The AI challenges your rounding once and you defend it.
options.stem: ask what the council actually needs → plan the report → research a real figure with the AI (verify it) → round and explain → test against the halfway line → share it on the wall

home: Two numbers differ by only 30,000. Which single seat can hold that whole difference?
Sort these into claim, evidence and conclusion: '4,697,000 is greater.' · 'The ten-thousands differ first: 90,000 beats 70,000.' · 'So the first reading is correct.'
When a partner's argument has a gap, what do you point to — the size of their voice, or the seat with no evidence?

claims: I can compare two numbers by the first place that differs.
I can state the value of a digit in any place up to the millions.
I can find the difference between two close large numbers.
I can tell a claim apart from the evidence that supports it.

independent.prompt: Two teams defend different numbers: 7,480,500 and 7,840,500. Which is the greater, and what is the exact gap the argument must explain?
independent.yes: Yes — the hundred-thousands places differ first: 800,000 beats 400,000, so 7,840,500 is greater, and the gap the argument must explain is 7,840,500 − 7,480,500 = 360,000.
independent.notYet: Not yet — scan from the greatest place to find the first difference, then work out the gap.

harder.prompt: Build the argument in one pass — claim, place, values, gap — for 8,241,000 against 8,214,000.
harder.answer: 8,241,000 is greater: the ten-thousands differ first — 40,000 beats 10,000 — and the gap is 27,000.
harder.hint: Claim, then the deciding place, then the two values, then the gap.

options.task: A 60-second argument presentation: state the claim, name the deciding place, give the two values, and land the gap — defending one census reading out loud.
options.stem: ask which reading the evidence supports → plan the claim-place-values-gap order → build the argument → test it on a partner's reading → share it and ask for the seal

options.task: An argument diagram a stranger could follow: the claim at the top, the place-value evidence on each branch, the gap your team closed, and the verdict at the bottom. Annotate every step.
options.stem: ask what the argument must show → plan the branches → draft the evidence → test it on a classmate (they must repeat the claim) → share it at the seal desk

options.task: A 90-second debate clip: record your argument, then ask the AI to pose three hard questions and answer each one on camera, yourself. The clip is your argument — never the AI's.
options.stem: ask what the argument is → plan the clip → record the argument → let the AI challenge it (answer every question yourself) → test the answers → share it on the wall
